results.title: نيمار يعلن نهاية مشواره مع منتخب البرازيل بعد 16 عامًا
results.description:
أعلن النجم البرازيلي نيمار جونيور نهاية مشواره الدولي مع منتخب البرازيل، بعد مسيرة استمرت 16 عامًا، منذ ظهوره الأول بقميص «السيليساو» عام 2010.

وقال نيمار في تصريحات للصحفيين: «أعتقد أن مشواري مع منتخب البرازيل قد انتهى. لقد كتبت صفحة من التاريخ معه، وأنا سعيد للغاية بذلك».

وأضاف: «لقد منحت المنتخب كل قلبي وكل حياتي، وكنت دائمًا أقاتل من أجل القميص الأصفر، لكنني أعتقد أنني لم أعد أرغب في الاستمرار».

وشارك نيمار مع المنتخب البرازيلي في بطولة كأس العالم 2026، وسجل هدفًا من ركلة جزاء خلال خسارة بلاده أمام النرويج بنتيجة 2-1 في دور الـ16.

وخاض نيمار 130 مباراة دولية بقميص البرازيل، سجل خلالها 80 هدفًا وصنع 59 تمريرة حاسمة، ليصبح أحد أبرز اللاعبين في تاريخ المنتخب البرازيلي.

ويواصل نيمار حاليًا مسيرته مع نادي سانتوس البرازيلي، الذي شهد انطلاقته في عالم كرة القدم قبل انتقاله إلى الملاعب الأوروبية.
creator: اليوم- ريو دي جانيرو

results.title: First test of ‘pilot zones’ in south Lebanon lays bare difficulties
results.description: First test of ‘pilot zones’ in south Lebanon lays bare difficulties The rollout of the first zone in the south Lebanese village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh last week offered a glimpse of a strained and complex process. Wednesday 29/07/2026 Lebanese soldiers stand guard in the town of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, after the withdrawal of Israeli forces, in southern Lebanon, July 26, 2026. ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYEH, Lebanon A US-brokered plan for Israel to withdraw gradually from occupied areas of southern Lebanon in exchange for the disarmament of the Iran-backed Hezbollah militia is off to a painfully slow start. To the US, the “pilot zone programme” is the centrepiece of a June 26 framework deal intended to end the war between Israel and Hezbollah, and establish peaceful ties between Israel and Lebanon. But Hezbollah itself still refuses to give up its weapons. And on the ground, the rollout of the first zone in the south Lebanese village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh last week offered a glimpse of a strained and complex process that will be no easier to repeat elsewhere. A senior Lebanese military official, who requested anonymity in order to speak freely, said it had taken weeks of US-brokered negotiations with Israel and days of military operations to establish the first zone in a single village. The agreement links Israel’s progressive withdrawal to the “verified disarmament” of Hezbollah — which is not a party to the deal, has refused to give up its arsenal, and has raised the prospect of internal strife if the state tries to disarm it by force. With such operational and political challenges ahead, the Lebanese military official and two foreign security officials said they expected it to take more than a year to secure Israel’s full withdrawal from Lebanon. Two days after the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, Hezbollah dragged Lebanon into the war by firing at Israel. Israeli forces responded with aerial bombardments reaching as far as Beirut, and by seizing a strip of land extending about 10 km deep into southern Lebanon. Even after a ceasefire last month, Israeli troops remained in the zone, razing villages and ordering residents who had fled not to return. The US began mediating talks between Lebanon and Israel in mid-April, and setting out the pilot zone programme in early June. More than six weeks later, Lebanese soldiers deployed to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh to implement the first zone after Israeli forces pulled back. Within hours, Israeli units still stationed hundreds of metres away in an adjacent village accused Lebanese troops of deploying too close, and fired warning shots to keep them back. An Israeli military official said troops were adjusting their “force posture” in the first pilot zone, without saying whether those who had withdrawn from Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh had left Lebanon altogether or redeployed to other parts of the south. The Lebanese troops spent two days clearing rubble and accompanying paramedics into the village to recover the bodies of Hezbollah fighters. On July 24, they finally allowed displaced residents to return, in carefully managed convoys. Most homes were too badly damaged from bombing for anyone to stay. Mayor Abed Ezzedin said around half of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh was in ruins, and reconstruction seemed far away. “What kind of pilot zone are we talking about? And what kind of security and safety? There are still 70 or 80 occupied villages,” he said. “If they (Israeli troops) are going to withdraw from one village while remaining on the edge of the next — we can’t do that. It won’t work. And what about the reconstruction we keep talking about? Without security and peace of mind, we can’t rebuild. We cannot lay a single stone on top of another in Zawtar.” Disarmament quandary Israeli troops remain stationed in a semicircle of towns to the north and east of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, the strategic Beaufort Castle on a commanding ridge just 6 km to the east, and dozens of villages further south. A key test of Lebanon’s willingness to disarm Hezbollah in exchange for more Israeli withdrawals could lie a few kilometres away, along a mountain ridge known as Ali Taher. Hezbollah is suspected of operating a command centre and weapons stores there, Lebanese security sources told Reuters. Hassan Jouni, a Lebanese analyst and retired general, said it was unlikely Israeli troops would withdraw from any more nearby positions “until the problem of Ali Taher is resolved” — either with Israel capturing the ridge or Lebanese troops clearing out Hezbollah weapons stores. Jouni noted that the June 26 deal does not set a timeline for either withdrawal or disarmament — and said disarming Hezbollah by force could, at worst, trigger civil war. Under the deal, disarmament must be verified by a third party to enable the Israeli military to “progressively redeploy out of Lebanese territory”. Neither a third party nor a mechanism for verification has been established, Jouni said. “The timeline for the Israeli occupation, based on this formula, will take a long time.” To speed the process, Lebanon intends to propose in talks with Israel next week that the occupied zone be divided into two or three large pilot zones encompassing dozens of towns, instead of Israel withdrawing village by village, the Lebanese military official said. But Israeli officials have said troops will remain in southern Lebanon as long as necessary, and residents of Israeli-occupied land doubt they will ever see their hometowns again. “How is Israel going to withdraw? It’s not that simple. They did the impossible to get in here; they aren’t just going to leave overnight,” said Zeinab Loubani, a 54-year-old mother displaced from a town near Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh. “I’m telling you, I don’t believe it for a second. It’s all just talk ... There’s nothing left to hope for.” Difficult to replicate After deploying last week, the Lebanese army initially prevented residents from entering Zawtar al-Gharbiya while it carried out search and sweep operations, before allowing locals to check their homes in recent days. Israeli tank tracks were still visible on the ground, while Hebrew writing was seen on the wall of one home. The deployment is a major test for the Lebanese state, with experts expressing doubt over authorities’ ability to disarm Hezbollah, which opposes the deal with Israel and refuses to surrender its weapons. Military expert Fadi Daoud said that the Lebanese army’s success in Zawtar al-Gharbiya was based on a “particular equation: a small area, relative calm, strong political symbolism and direct US pressure”. But the retired Lebanese army general said it would be tough to replicate “in broader and more complex areas”, particularly if Hezbollah sticks to its stance. The biggest challenge will be when the army receives “information on tunnels or weapons depots” belonging to the group and will have to decide to go in even if Hezbollah objects, he added, noting the military lacks clear legal authorisation to inspect private properties.

results.title: Tech hub to opera stage: Hefei gives Chinese opera digital lease on life
results.description: BEIJING , July 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A news report from China.org.cn: Better known for its high-tech industries and new-energy vehicles, Hefei, the capital of Anhui province in eastern China, is charting an unconventional course. Home to 10 million residents, this tech-driven city is striving to become a hub for opera culture, while harnessing modern innovation to keep traditional arts thriving. Redefining its urban competitiveness by blending cutting-edge tech with cultural traditions, Hefei launched the "Hundred Operas in Anhui — Starry Hefei" initiative in 2025. The project promotes traditional Chinese opera and aims to build the city into a core hub for national art exchange. Since its launch, 36 opera genres from across China have staged 101 performances in Hefei, complemented by 150 local Anhui troupes. Over 400 renowned actors have performed, including 53 recipients of the Plum Blossom Prize — China's highest theatrical honor. Impressive statistics highlight this revival: All shows sold out instantly, and the performances boasted an 86% occupancy rate. Tickets started at just 10 yuan ($1.60), greatly boosting accessibility for audiences. Leveraging an "opera tourism" model, ticket stubs grant free entry to world-class heritage sites like Mount Huangshan and Hefei's core attractions. Over 74,000 visitors have enjoyed immersive "opera and scenery" tours, boosting regional consumption. Crucially, the initiative has resonated deeply with Generation Z. Individuals under 40 account for 73.9% of the audience, with those under 30 reaching 44.4%. This stemmed from campus outreach programs that bring traditional arts into student life. "Ever since I started school here, I've wanted to experience Anhui's opera culture," said Yu Haoshen, a student from Inner Mongolia. "The initiative allows me to enjoy wonderful performances from all over the country without having to travel around." Furthermore, the project has attracted over 80 foreign nationals from more than a dozen countries, bridging language barriers. In 2026, Hefei partnered with China Media Group for the Opera Soulmate Conference, further engaging youth globally. The city is also planning to break ground on the China Opera Museum. Meanwhile, Hefei is utilizing its technological advantages to build a digital ecosystem for traditional opera supported by the Anhui Hundred Operas Center and six professional theaters. results.title: أوروبا تواجه اختباراً جديداً.. تراجع حاد في احتياطيات الغاز
results.description: سجلت احتياطيات الغاز في ألمانيا وهولندا انخفاضاً قياسياً، مما يعكس الضغوط المستمرة على أسواق الطاقة الأوروبية، إذ وصلت مستويات التخزين إلى أدنى معدلاتها مع اقتراب موسم التدفئة الشتوي. هبوط الخزانات ووفقاً لبيانات رابطة مشغلي البنية التحتية للغاز في أوروبا، بلغ حجم الغاز المخزن في ألمانيا حتى نهاية 26 يوليو الجاري نحو 10.1 مليار متر مكعب، بنسبة امتلاء 46.19%، وهي الأدنى منذ بدء الرصد. أما في هولندا، فتراجعت نسبة الامتلاء إلى 35.34% مع وجود نحو 4.5 مليار متر مكعب، وهو أدنى مستوى منذ بدء جمع البيانات في 2011.وفي بلجيكا، انخفضت نسبة امتلاء مخازن الغاز إلى 32.14%، بإجمالي 0.22 مليار متر مكعب، وهو أدنى مستوى يسجل في هذا الوقت من العام منذ 2015. وعلى مستوى الاتحاد الأوروبي، بلغ متوسط امتلاء مرافق تخزين الغاز حتى 26 يوليو نحو 55.66% من إجمالي السعة التخزينية، بما يعادل 55.86 مليار متر مكعب، وهو أدنى مستوى يسجل منذ 2021، ويقل بنحو 16 نقطة مئوية عن متوسط السنوات الخمس الماضية. ارتفاع المنافسة تأتي هذه التغيرات في ظل سعي الدول الأوروبية لإعادة ملء مخازنها استعداداً لفصل الشتاء، وسط استمرار عدم اليقين في أسواق الطاقة العالمية وارتفاع المنافسة على شحنات الغاز الطبيعي المسال. وقد دفعت هذه الظروف دول الاتحاد الأوروبي إلى تنويع مصادر وارداتها وتعزيز الاعتماد على الغاز المسال والطاقة المتجددة.وشهدت أوروبا خلال أزمة الطاقة في 2022 و2023 ارتفاعات قياسية في أسعار الغاز والكهرباء، مما دفع الحكومات إلى إطلاق برامج دعم واسعة لتحسين كفاءة التخزين وتجنب الأزمات في مواسم الشتاء القادمة.
creator: محمد الصاحي (القاهرة)
